name: Lixisenatide

lead: Lixisenatide (Lyxumia, Adlyxin) is a once-daily GLP-1 injection for type 2 diabetes, approved in the EU in 2013 and the US in 2016. In fat-loss discussion it appears as an older member of the GLP-1 class with a slight weight effect.

It activates GLP-1 receptors, boosting insulin release when glucose is high and slowing gastric emptying, which lowers appetite after meals and nudges intake and weight down. In the ELIXA trial it did not increase cardiovascular events relative to placebo.

paras: It is prescribed as a daily injection for diabetes, and is also sold combined with insulin glargine as Soliqua. It is not approved for obesity and has largely been replaced by longer-acting agents.
Nausea and vomiting are common; pancreatitis and allergic reactions are rarer. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Lixisenatide is a short-acting daily GLP-1 injection that lowers appetite after meals, giving a slight weight reduction toward a leaner body. Diabetes trials showed small weight reductions, and it plays a minor role next to newer GLP-1 drugs.

lead: Lixisenatide (Lyxumia in the EU, Adlyxin in the US) is a once-daily injectable short-acting GLP-1 receptor agonist for type 2 diabetes, created by Zealand Pharma of Denmark and licensed to Sanofi in 2003.[1] It was approved in the EU in February 2013 and in the US in July 2016.[1] It is also marketed with insulin glargine in a fixed-ratio combination called Soliqua.[2]

In appearance-focused communities, GLP-1 drugs are discussed as a route to fat loss, and so to a leaner face and body. Lixisenatide sits at the modest end of that class: it slows gastric emptying and lowers appetite, and trials in people with diabetes report small average weight reductions alongside its glucose effects.[3][4] It is not approved for obesity, and newer once-weekly agents have taken most of the attention.

The research base is mostly diabetes trials. In ELIXA, a placebo-controlled trial in 6,068 patients with type 2 diabetes and a recent acute coronary event, lixisenatide neither raised nor lowered major cardiovascular events relative to placebo.[5][6] A 2024 phase 2 trial also tested it in early Parkinson's disease.[7]

paras: Lixisenatide is indicated as an adjunct to diet and exercise for adults with type 2 diabetes. In the EU its use is authorised alongside oral glucose-lowering drugs and/or basal insulin when diet and exercise alone do not give adequate control.[1][2] The Soliqua combination is indicated for adults with type 2 diabetes.[2] Because it is short acting, it mainly lowers glucose after meals, with less effect on overnight and fasting glucose than longer-acting class members.[8]

All GLP-1 receptor agonists share actions that include slowing gastric emptying and reducing calorie intake and body weight.[8] Reviews of the class describe lixisenatide as producing smaller weight and HbA1c reductions than exenatide or liraglutide in head-to-head comparisons, while causing fewer adverse events.[9] Lixisenatide has not been developed or approved as an obesity treatment, and the large weight-loss trials that drive current interest in the class used other molecules.[3]

Lixisenatide binds and activates the GLP-1 receptor. This increases insulin release from pancreatic beta cells when blood glucose is high, suppresses glucagon, and slows gastric emptying, which blunts the glucose rise after meals.[1][8]

It is a 44-amino-acid peptide derived from the first 39 residues of exendin-4, a peptide first found in Gila monster venom, with one proline omitted and six lysines added at the end.[1] After subcutaneous injection it shows linear pharmacokinetics and a half-life of roughly 2-3 hours, which is why it is dosed daily and acts chiefly on mealtime glucose.[9]

Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, headache and dizziness were each reported by at least 5% of users.[1] A systematic analysis of GLP-1 agonist trials found gastrointestinal events to be the most commonly reported adverse events across the class.[10] Less common events include pancreatitis (about 0.2%) and anaphylaxis (about 0.1%); hypoglycemia can occur when combined with insulin or sulfonylureas.[1] Acute kidney injury linked to fluid loss has been reported, and antibodies can develop over time.[1][2] The product is not recommended in people with gastroparesis and can change the absorption timing of oral drugs.[1] The US label for the combination product carries warnings for hypersensitivity, pancreatitis, gallbladder disease and aspiration during anesthesia.[2]

Zealand Pharma discovered the compound and licensed it to Sanofi in 2003; the license was extended in 2010 to allow a combination with insulin glargine.[1] The European Commission approved Lyxumia in February 2013. The FDA accepted Sanofi's US application the same month, but Sanofi withdrew it in 2013 after discussions about cardiovascular safety data and planned to wait for the ELIXA trial, due in 2015.[1] After ELIXA reported, Sanofi resubmitted in September 2015 and the FDA approved Adlyxin in July 2016.[1][5]

The combination, LixiLan (later Soliqua), was submitted in December 2015. An FDA advisory committee voted 12-2 in its favour in May 2016, with reservations about the two pen formulations, and the decision was delayed by three months in August 2016.[1] Patent protection lapsed in 2020, and the product is described as discontinued in some markets, including the US brand in 2023 according to an AI-generated encyclopedia summary.[1][11]

ELIXA randomized 6,068 patients with type 2 diabetes and a recent myocardial infarction or unstable angina to lixisenatide or placebo and was designed to assess cardiovascular safety; major cardiovascular events were not significantly different between groups.[5][6] Meta-analyses of GLP-1 agonist cardiovascular outcome trials place ELIXA among the neutral studies, while some other class members showed cardiovascular benefit.[12][13]

In the GetGoal phase 3 program, lixisenatide added to metformin, sulfonylureas, pioglitazone or basal insulin lowered HbA1c versus placebo, with a pronounced effect on post-meal glucose.[9][11] A mixed-treatment comparison of GLP-1 agonists examined efficacy and safety across the class.[14] Fixed-ratio insulin glargine/lixisenatide combinations have been tested against other regimens in trials such as LixiLan JP-O1 in Japan and Soli-D in China.[15][16] Smaller mechanistic trials examined effects on glycaemic variability, chylomicron triglyceride clearance and gastric emptying.[17][18]

In neurology, a 2024 phase 2 randomized trial in 156 people with early Parkinson's disease compared lixisenatide with placebo over 12 months on motor disability scores and reported less progression with lixisenatide, with gastrointestinal side effects more common.[7][19] Preclinical work shows lixisenatide and liraglutide cross the blood-brain barrier and promote neurogenesis in rodents.[20]

Lixisenatide is prescription-only in the US, UK, EU and Canada.[1] It is rarely discussed in looksmaxxing forums compared with semaglutide and tirzepatide, which have larger weight-loss effects and obesity approvals. Its relevance to the wider conversation is as an earlier member of the GLP-1 family whose trials helped establish the class's cardiovascular safety record.[12]
